# Living Project Documentation

Use this capability to find the document that settles a reader's engineering
question and keep its answer true as the project changes. A plan records
intent. Living documentation describes the behavior, constraints and
procedures that actually hold. Update their owning pages in place. In a Git
project, commits and pull requests carry the history of changes and checks.
The [OKF v0.3 specification](https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format/blob/527e81aff55992be21507e97004286789126f88c/SPEC.md)
defines the bundle format. Here, `docs/` means the project's documentation root.

When migrating a populated collection, start at the project's published entry
point and follow [Assess the collection](./references/bootstrapping.md#assess-the-collection).
Consult worked examples when a particular placement or recovery choice is
unclear. Open the validator instructions when ready to check the edited root.

The requirement keywords used in this skill and its references follow
[RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119.html).

## Organizing a bundle

See [documentation-structure.md](./references/documentation-structure.md) for:

- authoring an OKF v0.3 concept and distinguishing format requirements from this skill's discovery defaults
- choosing the subject that owns a decision, reviewing its page type, and routing readers from a subject index or glossary

See [conventions-and-operations.md](./references/conventions-and-operations.md) for:

- placing a team's engineering choice, an implementation guarantee or an architectural boundary
- tracing permission, activation, verification and recovery when several procedures share an authority

## Adopting or migrating documentation

See [bootstrapping.md](./references/bootstrapping.md) for:

- starting with a single reader question in a new project
- migrating an existing collection to OKF, including a tree that already passes validation, or carrying out an explicitly format-only request
- designing the layout from questions in handoffs and callers, checking each answer and its limits at the destination, and reporting the questions and checks still open

See [cross-references.md](./references/cross-references.md) for:

- settling support for published paths and fragments, updating callers and checking record identifiers
- making navigation work both inside the checkout and in an exported bundle

The [Scheduler migration](./assets/scheduler-migration.md#target-and-evidence)
compares a heading repair and a subject split. Its
[rollback procedure](./assets/docs-example/operating/deployment.md#rolling-back)
shows which steps stay together.

## Consulting and maintaining docs

See [consulting-and-upkeep.md](./references/consulting-and-upkeep.md) for:

- consulting relevant owners before a plan and tracing dependent readers
- following a question from real entry points before and after a move, including the exception that changes the answer

See [validators.md](./references/validators.md) for:

- running one whole-root check for OKF conformance and engineering rules from the first day of migration
- interpreting evidence warnings and the editorial type list, using focused checks and qualifying a standalone export

=== README.md ===
     1	# inkwell
     2	
     3	A small hosted CMS: an author manages one or more customer sites, works
     4	through a site's posts, and publishes one. Publishing writes a revision and
     5	calls the site's deploy hook. See `AGENTS.md` for the shape of the product and
     6	[the engineering manual](docs/index.md) for publishing and delivery. The manual ships
     7	as the contents of `docs/`. Short excerpts from our own source and tests may
     8	ship in the manual with their source path and revision. Support records are under `support/`.
     9	
    10	## Getting started
    11	
    12	```bash
    13	npm install
    14	npx playwright install chromium # once per machine — the browser test project needs it
    15	npm run db:generate # only after changing server/db/schema.ts
    16	npm run db:migrate # creates/updates server/db/data/inkwell.db
    17	npm run dev:api # in one terminal
    18	npm run dev # in another
    19	```
    20	
    21	The dev server proxies `/api` to the API at `http://localhost:8787` — see
    22	`vite.config.ts`. The API seeds a few demo sites and posts on first run
    23	against an empty database. It seeds no revisions: one is written the first
    24	time you publish something, which is also the first thing the Revisions
    25	screen has to show.
    26	
    27	`GET /api/me` reports the signed-in author. In a real deploy that comes from
    28	whatever fronts the console — it forwards the author as `x-forwarded-user`
    29	and `x-forwarded-user-name` — and locally, with nothing in front of the API,
    30	it falls back to a development author so the console still knows who you are.
    31	
    32	## Commands
    33	
    34	| Command                | What it does                                                                                                                         |
    35	| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
    36	| `npm run dev`          | Serves the SPA locally with hot reload.                                                                                              |
    37	| `npm run dev:api`      | Starts the Hono API on `PORT` (default `8787`).                                                                                      |
    38	| `npm run build`        | Type-checks, then builds the production SPA bundle.                                                                                  |
    39	| `npm run preview`      | Serves a build produced by `npm run build`.                                                                                          |
    40	| `npm run format`       | Rewrites the project in place to its house style.                                                                                    |
    41	| `npm run format:check` | Reports formatting drift without rewriting anything.                                                                                 |
    42	| `npm run lint`         | Lints the whole project with ESLint.                                                                                                 |
    43	| `npm run typecheck`    | Type-checks both the SPA and the API/server projects.                                                                                |
    44	| `npm test`             | Runs the Vitest suite: the Node project (SPA logic, the API, `shared/`) and the browser project (real-DOM component tests) together. |
    45	| `npm run db:generate`  | Generates a SQL migration from `server/db/schema.ts` into `server/db/migrations/`.                                                   |
    46	| `npm run db:migrate`   | Applies pending migrations to the SQLite file at `DATABASE_PATH` (default `server/db/data/inkwell.db`).                              |
    47	
    48	## Layout
    49	
    50	- `src/routes/` — the three real screens (`PostListPage`, `PostEditorPage`,
    51	  `RevisionsPage`) and the `Layout` shell they render inside, which owns the
    52	  persistent sidebar and identifies the signed-in author to analytics.
    53	- `src/components/` — reusable pieces: `Card`, `Button`, `Sidebar`,
    54	  `ConsentBanner`, `PublishToast`.
    55	- `src/lib/` — the API client, the TanStack Query client, consent state, and
    56	  the Amplitude wrapper.
    57	- `src/queries/` — TanStack Query option factories, one export per file.
    58	- `server/` — the Hono API, the Drizzle schema, and the generated SQL
    59	  migrations under `server/db/migrations/`.

# Conventions and Operations

## Placing a project rule

Where a violation appears helps identify the reader who needs the rule. A
client receiving a missing field encounters a contract violation. A reviewer
checking directory layout is applying a Convention, even if a linter enforces
it. An operator diagnosing a queue backlog needs the Architecture to identify
the producer and consumer before consulting a recovery Procedure.

**Guidelines:**

- SHOULD place an observable guarantee in its Specification and a team's choice among conforming practices in its Convention.
- MUST keep the constraint beside its reasoning and link to its existing owner when already documented. A project with architectural decision records MAY link the original record for provenance.

## Permission and execution

A release operator activates a rollout. A device operator checks the
installation and restores service if verification fails. Both procedures can
depend on the same permission to release. When one operator carries out a
single task, a locally scoped permission check can fit directly in its steps.

**Guidelines:**

- SHOULD extract a Policy when several entry points depend on a permission rule that changes independently.
- MUST identify the adopted scope, exception authority and reopening conditions, and connect every affected entry point, including manual and emergency paths, to the actual authority.
- SHOULD give operators separate procedures when their tasks have different prerequisites, success signals or recovery actions.
- MUST state the local stop condition beside a consequential step. A successful recovery command establishes what ran. Permission to run it comes from the project's authority.
- MUST NOT invent an approver or independent permission rule to populate a type.

## Contributor routes

A contributor guide can direct a new maintainer to the setup procedure and a
reviewer to the same convention used by the linter. Each route leads to one
maintained rule.

**Guidelines:**

- SHOULD document each subject's scope and its nearest confusing neighbor. Give a tie-breaker a contributor can apply to a new claim and explain when to add a subject. For instance, a worker-pool cap belongs with dispatch internals unless it promises an outcome to callers.
- SHOULD link the placement convention from durable human and agent entry points and update it when responsibility moves. Link editable callers directly to their governing section.

1	# Migrating the Scheduler handbook
2	
3	“Please migrate the Scheduler engineering docs to OKF.” The example follows
4	the job outcomes, notification rules and release procedure through that change.
5	The trees show the paths involved. The [finished bundle](./docs-example/index.md)
6	also covers job creation, worker dispatch and contribution practices.
7	
8	## Before
9	
10	```text
11	docs/
12	├── index.md
13	├── specs/
14	│   └── jobs.md
15	└── guides/
16	    └── handbook.md
17	```
18	
19	The root offered **Specifications → Jobs** and **Guides → Handbook**.
20	Starting there, a new API client author asking “Can a cancelled job run
21	again if it still has retries?” had to guess the document type.
22	`specs/jobs.md#states` listed `cancelled` among the possible states.
23	Its retry section said “A failed job may be retried three times.” Neither
24	section answered the cancellation question.
25	
26	The handbook mixed three decisions.
27	
28	- **Notifications.** “A rule fires on a terminal state. Check the job states
29	  to decide which outcomes qualify.” Its link pointed to `../specs/jobs.md#states`.
30	- **Checking a release.** “Watch the claim rate for five minutes. Jobs
31	  waiting for a retry appear as queued. A job gets three tries in all.”
32	- **Undoing a release.** “Use the recorded previous revision. If a destructive
33	  contract migration already removed data, stop and hand the restore to
34	  on-call. Otherwise run `npm run deploy -- --revision <previous>`.”
35	
36	## Target and evidence
37	
38	Adding links to the handbook headings would shorten the operator's route.
39	It would still leave the API contract divided between the Jobs specification
40	and a release check. Changing the retry budget would require finding both
41	accounts. A subject entry for scheduling can give client authors the job
42	contract, while the operator can change the release check independently.
43	
44	The illustrative checkout's adopted decision defines when retries end.
45	The worker's transition table dispatches retries only on failure. The
46	cancellation test exercises the case where two retries remain. The
47	[exported state contract](./docs-example/scheduling/outcomes.md#states)
48	links the relevant decision and test excerpts so a reader can check exactly
49	what was decided and what the test observes.
50	
51	| Legacy passage or question                        | Destination and reason                                                                                                                                                                                 |
52	| ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
53	| Jobs / States and the missing cancellation answer | Move the state contract to Scheduling / Job outcomes. Add what happens on cancellation with retries left from the adopted decision.                                                                    |
54	| Jobs / Retries and Handbook / Checking a release  | Consolidate the conflicting counts at Job outcomes. Extract the public `queued` behavior from the runbook. Keep the five-minute claim-rate check in Deployment and link directly to the retry passage. |
55	| Handbook / Notifications                          | Move the rules to Notifications. Keep the decision to send a message here and point its state lookup directly to Job outcomes.                                                                         |
56	| Handbook / Undoing a release                      | Keep the rollback command, its authority and the stop/restore branch together in Deployment. An operator about to redeploy needs all three.                                                            |
57	
58	One client question remains open. How long after cancellation can an external
59	process keep writing? The transition test observes the job state and retry
60	queue. It measures no process shutdown time, and the adopted decision gives
61	no deadline. Record that clients cannot choose an output-read timeout from
62	this evidence. Leave the deadline out of the contract.
63	
64	## After
65	
66	```text
67	docs/
68	├── index.md
69	├── scheduling/
70	│   ├── index.md
71	│   ├── jobs.md
72	│   ├── outcomes.md
73	│   ├── attempts.md
74	│   └── dispatch.md
75	├── notifications.md
76	└── operating/
77	    └── deployment.md
78	```
79	
80	Replay the client's question from the [revised root](./docs-example/index.md).
81	**Scheduling → Which job states are terminal?** lands on “A cancelled job
82	receives no automatic retry, even if retries remain.” Someone starting at the
83	glossary with the dashboard term “Retries remaining” reaches the retry contract.
84	[Scheduling index](./docs-example/scheduling/index.md) · [Owning state contract](./docs-example/scheduling/outcomes.md#states) · [Dashboard term](./docs-example/glossary.md)
85	
86	Start again at the edited caller. [Notification rules](./docs-example/notifications.md#rules)
87	links “which states are terminal, including cancellation with retries left”
88	directly to the contract. [Verifying a release](./docs-example/operating/deployment.md#verifying-a-release)

# Migrating the Scheduler handbook

“Please migrate the Scheduler engineering docs to OKF.” The example follows
the job outcomes, notification rules and release procedure through that change.
The trees show the paths involved. The [finished bundle](./docs-example/index.md)
also covers job creation, worker dispatch and contribution practices.

## Before

```text
docs/
├── index.md
├── specs/
│   └── jobs.md
└── guides/
    └── handbook.md
```

The root offered **Specifications → Jobs** and **Guides → Handbook**.
Starting there, a new API client author asking “Can a cancelled job run
again if it still has retries?” had to guess the document type.
`specs/jobs.md#states` listed `cancelled` among the possible states.
Its retry section said “A failed job may be retried three times.” Neither
section answered the cancellation question.

The handbook mixed three decisions.

- **Notifications.** “A rule fires on a terminal state. Check the job states
  to decide which outcomes qualify.” Its link pointed to `../specs/jobs.md#states`.
- **Checking a release.** “Watch the claim rate for five minutes. Jobs
  waiting for a retry appear as queued. A job gets three tries in all.”
- **Undoing a release.** “Use the recorded previous revision. If a destructive
  contract migration already removed data, stop and hand the restore to
  on-call. Otherwise run `npm run deploy -- --revision <previous>`.”

## Target and evidence

Adding links to the handbook headings would shorten the operator's route.
It would still leave the API contract divided between the Jobs specification
and a release check. Changing the retry budget would require finding both
accounts. A subject entry for scheduling can give client authors the job
contract, while the operator can change the release check independently.

The illustrative checkout's adopted decision defines when retries end.
The worker's transition table dispatches retries only on failure. The
cancellation test exercises the case where two retries remain. The
[exported state contract](./docs-example/scheduling/outcomes.md#states)
links the relevant decision and test excerpts so a reader can check exactly
what was decided and what the test observes.

| Legacy passage or question                        | Destination and reason                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Jobs / States and the missing cancellation answer | Move the state contract to Scheduling / Job outcomes. Add what happens on cancellation with retries left from the adopted decision.                                                                    |
| Jobs / Retries and Handbook / Checking a release  | Consolidate the conflicting counts at Job outcomes. Extract the public `queued` behavior from the runbook. Keep the five-minute claim-rate check in Deployment and link directly to the retry passage. |
| Handbook / Notifications                          | Move the rules to Notifications. Keep the decision to send a message here and point its state lookup directly to Job outcomes.                                                                         |
| Handbook / Undoing a release                      | Keep the rollback command, its authority and the stop/restore branch together in Deployment. An operator about to redeploy needs all three.                                                            |

One client question remains open. How long after cancellation can an external
process keep writing? The transition test observes the job state and retry
queue. It measures no process shutdown time, and the adopted decision gives
no deadline. Record that clients cannot choose an output-read timeout from
this evidence. Leave the deadline out of the contract.

## After

```text
docs/
├── index.md
├── scheduling/
│   ├── index.md
│   ├── jobs.md
│   ├── outcomes.md
│   ├── attempts.md
│   └── dispatch.md
├── notifications.md
└── operating/
    └── deployment.md
```

Replay the client's question from the [revised root](./docs-example/index.md).
**Scheduling → Which job states are terminal?** lands on “A cancelled job
receives no automatic retry, even if retries remain.” Someone starting at the
glossary with the dashboard term “Retries remaining” reaches the retry contract.
[Scheduling index](./docs-example/scheduling/index.md) · [Owning state contract](./docs-example/scheduling/outcomes.md#states) · [Dashboard term](./docs-example/glossary.md)

Start again at the edited caller. [Notification rules](./docs-example/notifications.md#rules)
links “which states are terminal, including cancellation with retries left”
directly to the contract. [Verifying a release](./docs-example/operating/deployment.md#verifying-a-release)
now links to the retry passage and tells the operator to check the claim rate
before diagnosing a stall. At [Rolling back](./docs-example/operating/deployment.md#rolling-back),
someone who has already removed data encounters the stop and handoff before
the command.

Try placing a neighboring contract about the state a client sees while a
job waits for its first worker. Scheduling owns the state returned to the
client. Notifications owns whether a recipient is told about it. Two entry
points route contributors to that [placement rule](./docs-example/contributing/documentation.md#choose-a-subject).

| Project entry | Edited instruction                                                                                                     |
| ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `README.md`   | `When contributing docs, [choose the owning subject](./docs/contributing/documentation.md#choose-a-subject).`          |
| `AGENTS.md`   | `Before adding a contract, consult the [placement convention](./docs/contributing/documentation.md#choose-a-subject).` |

supported. The [retained heading](./docs-example/index.md#specifications)
links to the subject owners. The project approved retiring the two internal
legacy page paths after switching their editable callers. Record those path
decisions alongside the change. The work record marks job outcomes,
notifications and release operations covered, with the shutdown-time
question unresolved. Job creation and dispatch still need their own reader
checks before the whole collection can be reported as migrated.

=== ./contributing/directory-structure.md ===
---
type: Convention
title: Directory structure
description: Module placement, import direction and route naming for the API and worker.
---

# Directory Structure

The API and worker are the two deployable **Packages**. Each runs in its own
environment. This convention governs the modules each package contains or imports.

The general discipline — put shared logic at the lowest tier with more than one
caller, name a file for what it holds — belongs to the installed code-maintainability
capability. What follows is this repository's own tiers and paths, which nothing
outside it could infer.

## The Tree

```text
<root>
├── api/                       # the API package: creates jobs, serves the dashboard
│   ├── routes/<route>/
│   │   ├── _components/       # used by this route only
│   │   └── handler.ts
│   └── _/                     # feature-agnostic modules shared across routes
├── worker/                    # the worker package: claims jobs, runs attempts
└── shared/                    # the few modules both packages import
```

## Tiers

A module sits at the lowest tier that has more than one caller, and MUST NOT be
promoted in anticipation of a second — a module promoted early is one every package
pays to read while one of them uses it.

`shared/` MUST stay deliberate. A module there is imported by two deployables that
run in separate processes, so a change to it changes both at once. It belongs there only
when both packages need the same _behaviour_, never merely the same shape.

The import direction is one-way: `api/` and `worker/` MAY import `shared/`; `shared/`
MUST NOT import either, and the two packages MUST NOT import each other. Each
production package contains only its own modules and shared dependencies. A
cross-package import can compile in the checkout and fail in the deployed process.

## Naming

A file is named for what it holds, in kebab-case; a directory, for the thing its files
are about. A route directory MUST match the URL segment it serves — the router derives
one from the other, so a mismatch is a 404 nobody can see in review.

`_`-prefixed directories are not routed. Anything under `routes/` without the prefix
becomes a URL, so a helper dropped there unprefixed is published.

# Placing a documentation change

## Choose a subject

Put a rule where the person making the decision would look for it:

- Scheduling owns a job's observable behavior and the worker mechanism that
  implements it. For a state returned to a caller, update the job contract.
  For a change to how workers coordinate claims, update job dispatch.
- Notifications owns what a recipient receives. If a change determines
  whether a job is terminal, scheduling owns that decision and notification
  rules link to it. If it determines whether to send a message about a
  terminal job, put it with notification rules.
- Operating owns the release operator's sequence, checks and stop conditions.
  Contributing owns practices for people changing the repository or its docs.

Add a subject when readers bring an independent question with no current
owner. Link it from the root, distinguish it from its nearest neighbor here,
and revise this rule if responsibility moves. Within a subject, add a local
index when readers need to choose between several questions.

=== ./notifications.md ===
---
type: Specification
title: Notifications
description: How terminal job outcomes reach channels, immediately or in a digest.
---

# Notifications

How someone finds out what happened. This domain covers the rules that turn an
outcome into a message, the channels those messages reach, and the digest that
collapses a run of them.

## Rules

A **Notification Rule** belongs to the account, not to a template, and selects the jobs it
cares about by template name and terminal state. Two rules matching the same job both
fire; the product does not deduplicate across rules, because each names its own
channel and suppressing one would silently drop a recipient.

A rule fires on a job's terminal state only. `queued` and `running` are not states a
rule can select, so a job that never finishes never notifies —
see [which states are terminal, including cancellation with retries left](./scheduling/outcomes.md#states).

## Channels

A **Channel** is an email address, webhook, or chat integration. A rule names
exactly one channel. A channel serves many rules, so disabling a channel
silences every rule pointing at it at once, and the rules stay enabled rather than
being rewritten.

A webhook channel is called at most once per message and is not retried. A delivery
that fails is recorded against the channel and visible in its history; the product
does not queue undelivered messages, because a webhook replayed an hour later reaches
an operator who has already moved on.

## Digests

# Directory Structure

The API and worker are the two deployable **Packages**. Each runs in its own
environment. This convention governs the modules each package contains or imports.

The general discipline — put shared logic at the lowest tier with more than one
caller, name a file for what it holds — belongs to the installed code-maintainability
capability. What follows is this repository's own tiers and paths, which nothing
outside it could infer.

## The Tree

```text
<root>
├── api/                       # the API package: creates jobs, serves the dashboard
│   ├── routes/<route>/
│   │   ├── _components/       # used by this route only
│   │   └── handler.ts
│   └── _/                     # feature-agnostic modules shared across routes
├── worker/                    # the worker package: claims jobs, runs attempts
└── shared/                    # the few modules both packages import
```

## Tiers

A module sits at the lowest tier that has more than one caller, and MUST NOT be
promoted in anticipation of a second — a module promoted early is one every package
pays to read while one of them uses it.

`shared/` MUST stay deliberate. A module there is imported by two deployables that
run in separate processes, so a change to it changes both at once. It belongs there only
when both packages need the same _behaviour_, never merely the same shape.

The import direction is one-way: `api/` and `worker/` MAY import `shared/`; `shared/`
MUST NOT import either, and the two packages MUST NOT import each other. Each
production package contains only its own modules and shared dependencies. A
cross-package import can compile in the checkout and fail in the deployed process.

## Naming

A file is named for what it holds, in kebab-case; a directory, for the thing its files
are about. A route directory MUST match the URL segment it serves — the router derives
one from the other, so a mismatch is a 404 nobody can see in review.

`_`-prefixed directories are not routed. Anything under `routes/` without the prefix
becomes a URL, so a helper dropped there unprefixed is published.

# Publishing a post

Publishing a post performs three steps, in order:

1. Write a `revisions` row — a snapshot of the post's title and body at the
   moment of publish.
2. Flip the post's `status` to `published`.
3. Call the site's `deployHookUrl`.

## What happens in one transaction

Steps 1 and 2 are one transaction: either both happen or neither does. A test
in `server/db/queries.test.ts` exercises the partial-failure case directly —
it fails the transaction after the revision insert and confirms the revision
is gone and the post is still `draft`.

Step 3 is best-effort. By the time it runs, the revision and the published
status are already committed, so rolling them back because a webhook timed
out would throw away real work over a problem that's usually transient and,
worse, outside this app's control entirely. **A failed hook does not undo
the publish.**

The publish response carries `deployTriggered: boolean`, and the editor
(`PostEditorPage.tsx`) shows the author which case they're in: a success
toast when the hook fired, an error toast telling them they may need to
trigger the rebuild themselves when it didn't. See
[recovering from a missed build](./recovery.md) for what that means
operationally.

## The deploy hook call

A call is a bare `POST` to the site's `deployHookUrl` with no body. A `2xx`
response counts as success; anything else — a non-2xx status or a thrown
error — is retried.

`triggerDeployHook` (`server/deploy-hook.ts`) retries twice more on failure —
three attempts in total — with a linear backoff between them (250ms, then
500ms). That's tuned for a cold serverless function taking a moment to wake
up, not for a target that's genuinely down: three attempts a few hundred
milliseconds apart won't save a publish from a deploy hook that's been
deleted or misconfigured.

When every attempt fails, the failure is logged at `error` — there's no
error tracker on the API side to hand it to instead — and the call returns
`{ ok: false }` rather than throwing, so the publish route above always gets
a definite answer either way.

## What accepted does not promise

[Release 17's receipt](./receipts/hook-17.txt) is `acme`'s record of one
deploy hook call: a `202`, which `response.ok` treats as success the same as
any other `2xx`.

A `2xx` response means the host *accepted* the request to rebuild, not that
the rebuild has finished. How long the site's host actually takes to make
the new page live afterward is that host's own build pipeline — outside this
app's control, and not something any test or log here observes. Nothing in
this app promises a time-to-live after acceptance; a caller needing that
number has to get it from the host.

# Revisions

Every publish [writes a revision](./publishing.md) — a snapshot of the
post's title and body at that moment. A draft save never does: it updates
the post in place without adding a snapshot, so only what actually went out
shows up here.

## Grouping and titles

The screen groups a site's revisions by the post they belong to. Each
group's heading uses the post's *current* title; each snapshot inside it
uses the title that was saved *at that publish*. Renaming a post relabels
the group without rewriting its history, so an older snapshot can show a
title the post no longer has.

## Ordering

Within a site, revisions come back newest first. `created_at` only resolves
to the second, and two publishes inside the same second are ordinary, so
ties break on the revision's `id`, descending — the snapshot written later
(the higher id) sorts first. `GET /sites/:siteSlug/revisions` orders by
`(created_at desc, id desc)` for exactly this reason.

## A failed deploy hook changes nothing here

[A failed deploy hook doesn't undo a publish](./publishing.md#what-happens-in-one-transaction):
the post and its revision are already committed either way. A revision for
a release whose hook never fired looks exactly like one whose hook
succeeded — this screen has no way to tell you which; see
[recovering from a missed build](./recovery.md) if that's the question.

# Recovering from a missed build

The author, or anyone handling support for that site, runs this once a
publish has already
[reported `deployTriggered: false`](./publishing.md#what-happens-in-one-transaction).
The post is published and its revision is written either way — this
procedure is only about getting the site to actually rebuild.

## Steps

1. Open the site's hosting dashboard and check its deploy queue for this
   publication.
2. If a build for it is already queued or running, stop here and follow
   that build instead. Triggering another one risks a second, redundant
   rebuild racing the first.
3. Otherwise, trigger one rebuild directly from the host dashboard.

Publishing the post again is a fallback, not the first move: it writes
another revision and calls the deploy hook again, which only helps if the
hook call itself — not the host's build queue — was the problem.

# inkwell

A small hosted CMS: an author manages one or more customer sites, works
through a site's posts, and publishes one. Publishing writes a revision and
calls the site's deploy hook. See `AGENTS.md` for the shape of the product and
[the engineering manual](docs/index.md) for publishing and delivery. The manual ships
as the contents of `docs/`. Short excerpts from our own source and tests may
ship in the manual with their source path and revision. Support records are under `support/`.

## Getting started

```bash
npm install
npx playwright install chromium # once per machine — the browser test project needs it
npm run db:generate # only after changing server/db/schema.ts
npm run db:migrate # creates/updates server/db/data/inkwell.db
npm run dev:api # in one terminal
npm run dev # in another
```

The dev server proxies `/api` to the API at `http://localhost:8787` — see
`vite.config.ts`. The API seeds a few demo sites and posts on first run
against an empty database. It seeds no revisions: one is written the first
time you publish something, which is also the first thing the Revisions
screen has to show.

`GET /api/me` reports the signed-in author. In a real deploy that comes from
whatever fronts the console — it forwards the author as `x-forwarded-user`
and `x-forwarded-user-name` — and locally, with nothing in front of the API,
it falls back to a development author so the console still knows who you are.

## Commands

| Command                | What it does                                                                                                                         |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `npm run dev`          | Serves the SPA locally with hot reload.                                                                                              |
| `npm run dev:api`      | Starts the Hono API on `PORT` (default `8787`).                                                                                      |
| `npm run build`        | Type-checks, then builds the production SPA bundle.                                                                                  |
| `npm run preview`      | Serves a build produced by `npm run build`.                                                                                          |
| `npm run format`       | Rewrites the project in place to its house style.                                                                                    |
| `npm run format:check` | Reports formatting drift without rewriting anything.                                                                                 |
| `npm run lint`         | Lints the whole project with ESLint.                                                                                                 |
| `npm run typecheck`    | Type-checks both the SPA and the API/server projects.                                                                                |
| `npm test`             | Runs the Vitest suite: the Node project (SPA logic, the API, `shared/`) and the browser project (real-DOM component tests) together. |
| `npm run db:generate`  | Generates a SQL migration from `server/db/schema.ts` into `server/db/migrations/`.                                                   |
| `npm run db:migrate`   | Applies pending migrations to the SQLite file at `DATABASE_PATH` (default `server/db/data/inkwell.db`).                              |

## Layout

- `src/routes/` — the three real screens (`PostListPage`, `PostEditorPage`,
  `RevisionsPage`) and the `Layout` shell they render inside, which owns the
  persistent sidebar and identifies the signed-in author to analytics.
- `src/components/` — reusable pieces: `Card`, `Button`, `Sidebar`,
  `ConsentBanner`, `PublishToast`.
- `src/lib/` — the API client, the TanStack Query client, consent state, and
  the Amplitude wrapper.
- `src/queries/` — TanStack Query option factories, one export per file.
- `server/` — the Hono API, the Drizzle schema, and the generated SQL
  migrations under `server/db/migrations/`.
- `shared/` — code imported by both the SPA and the API. Just the logger
  today.
- `docs/` — [what a failed hook means for a published revision](docs/guides/desk.md#missed-build).
- `.github/workflows/` — the checks that run on every pull request.

## Environment variables

See `.env.example`. Every one of them is optional in local development — a
missing Amplitude key or Sentry DSN just disables that feature rather than
failing to start.

Three are build-time only and belong to whatever runs `npm run build` for a
real deploy rather than to a developer's machine: `SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN`,
`SENTRY_ORG` and `SENTRY_PROJECT`. Without them the build still succeeds and
still emits source maps; it just doesn't upload them, which is why a
production stack trace from a build that lacked the token stays minified.

## Contributing

misunderstood requirement while it's still cheap to redirect, rather than
after the diff exists. A pull request is reviewed by someone other than the
person who wrote it, and merges only once that review is clean and the
commands above pass.

# AGENTS.md

## What this project is

A small hosted CMS. An author signs in — session handling lives outside this
cut of the product, so there's no sign-in screen here and the API reads who
the author is from what the session boundary forwards — and manages one or
more customer sites from the same account. Each site has its own posts;
opening a post gives you a full-page editor with a title, a body, a draft
save, and a publish action. Publishing snapshots the post into a revision and
calls the site's deploy hook so the static build actually goes out.

The sidebar carries two sections, Posts and Revisions, and shows which author
is signed in underneath them. There's no dashboard, no settings page, and no
onboarding flow yet.

## How the code is organized

`src/` is the SPA: `routes/` holds the three real screens (a per-site post
list, the post editor, and that site's revision history) plus the shell they
render inside, `components/` holds
what's reusable across more than one of them, `lib/` is where a cross-cutting
concern — the API client, the query client, consent, analytics — gets exactly
one home, and `queries/` holds the TanStack Query option factories, one
export per file, grouped by the resource they read or write rather than by
the screen that happens to call them first.

`server/` is the API: a thin Hono app in `app.ts`, the Drizzle schema and its
generated SQL migrations under `db/`, and the deploy-hook call in its own
module because it's the one thing in this app that talks to somebody else's
infrastructure and needed a retry policy to go with it.

`shared/` is the one thing both sides import — right now just the logger.
Anything that earns a place there has to make sense with zero DOM APIs and
zero Node APIs in scope, since it's bundled into the browser build and run
directly by the API both.

Read `README.md` for the full command list and layout before touching either
side.

## How changes are made

Nothing lands on `main` directly. Sketch the change and get it agreed on
before writing it — a plan is a much cheaper place to catch a misunderstood
requirement than a finished diff is. A pull request gets reviewed by someone
other than whoever wrote it, and it merges once that review has nothing left
to raise and the checks in `README.md` are green.

The [maintenance decisions](maintenance/decisions.md) record agreed work.

Keep a pull request to the problem it set out to solve. Renaming something
you noticed in passing, reformatting a file you didn't otherwise touch, or
folding in an unrelated fix makes the diff harder to review for the same
reason it was harder to write: two changes being reasoned about as though
they were one. Split it, or leave the rest for its own change.

## Publishing, briefly

Publish does three things, in order: write a revision snapshot of the post's
current title and body, flip the post to `published`, and call the site's
deploy hook. The first two are one transaction; the third is best-effort — a
site's deploy hook lives on somebody else's infrastructure, and a slow or
briefly-down webhook shouldn't cost the author their published content. The
API reports whether the deploy actually fired (`deployTriggered`) and the
editor tells the author which case they're in, rather than pretending publish
either fully succeeded or fully failed. `docs/deploy-hooks.md` has the retry
policy and the reasoning behind it; read it before changing
`server/deploy-hook.ts` or the publish route that calls it.

The revision written by step one is what the Revisions screen reads back, so
a change to what publish snapshots changes what that screen shows.

# Consulting and Upkeep

## Consult before planning

A change to retry timing can invalidate both the scheduler's contract and an
operator's procedure for recognizing a stuck job. The index identifies the
initial owners. Their preconditions and authority links reveal other readers.

**Guidelines:**

- MUST consult the index to locate unfamiliar subjects before planning a change. Follow precise caller links directly and trace the dependencies whose claims the change would invalidate.
- SHOULD stop reading when the routes establish that the change affects no documented claim. Revisit that conclusion if implementation reveals a dependency.

## Find the affected claim

| Change                                            | Consult                                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A metric changes eligibility, units or weighting  | Its Definition and the Specifications that consume it                        |
| A mode returns a different result or error        | Its result Specification and readers that present the value                  |
| Responsibility moves between components           | The Architecture, diagrams and operational diagnostics that use the boundary |
| A team changes an implementation practice         | Its Convention, counterexamples and enforcement                              |
| A release permission changes                      | The Policy and each entry point that relies on it                            |
| A command, prerequisite or success signal changes | Its Procedure and the caller's route to recovery                             |
| A term, file or heading moves                     | Glossary conventions, indexes, inbound links and external anchors            |

**Guidelines:**

- MUST correct an invalidated claim in the same change and update the routes that depend on it.
- SHOULD leave a page alone when the change preserves its claims and reading routes.

## Record what became true

An adopted target architecture and a deployed component can answer different
questions about the same service. A later contributor also needs to know why
an apparently workable alternative violates a settled constraint. When a retry
limit changes, replace the value and the reason for it on the governing page.
The commit shows the previous limit. The pull request holds the benchmark and
review discussion that led to the change.

**Guidelines:**

- MUST describe observable behavior in the present tense, identifying targets and illustrative examples explicitly.
- MUST put a settled constraint and its current rationale on the page that governs it. Include a rejected alternative when readers are likely to try it. Keep deliberation and run results with the commit or pull request that settled the change. Link that source when a current claim depends on it.
- MUST update the governing page in place. Do not append dated updates or create a page, registry or concept type for each verification run, rollout or decision.
- MUST retire obsolete guidance when a feature disappears and [settle support for affected routes](./cross-references.md#preserve-the-reading-route).
- SHOULD read each changed page on its own and exercise a boundary case from a consumer's or operator's entry point. Run the [documentation checks](./validators.md).

## Verify a reader's route

An on-call runbook links “Can I roll back?” to a release overview. The
overview links to “Rolling back,” where the operator learns to redeploy the
previous revision only while the data survives. After a destructive contract
migration, the operator must stop and use the restore procedure. Point the
runbook straight at “Rolling back.” Start again at the runbook: the operator
can skip the overview and stop at the same decision, with its exception.
Linking to a valid “Releasing” heading instead would lose that answer.

**Guidelines:**

- SHOULD sample real tasks before and after a substantial move. Record the question, starting path and fragment, pages and sections opened, owning answer, limiting condition and stopping point for each route.
- MUST exercise the root, the relevant subject index and representative callers such as a README, runbook or dependent concept. Follow the routes the export actually ships. A shortcut at the root can hide a missing choice at a subject index.
- MUST compare the link's promise to the actual passage, including exceptions. Repair a misleading label or heading, a missing local route or a detour through unrelated material. Keep a longer route when the reader genuinely needs both owners.
- MAY compare hops, distinct files or bytes opened to diagnose a detour. Count a file once per question and starting point when measuring whole-file exposure. Use the decision and its limits to judge the change.
